During the last decade the development of railway enterprise in Syria, has been for the slow East, almost phenomenal. There are, in all now, about 1300 kilometres of railraod, under exploitation. When we consider the comparatively limited area of the country covered by this netwrok of railway lines we find the ratio to be fairly important. We shall take the lines serverally in their chronological order of construction and at the same time give the actual conditions under which the different lines are working, their relation to the trade of the country, and their possibilities of development ; thus affording material of interest also to the general reader. Apart from the Hedjaz railway, al the railroads of Syria have been built by French companies, and this, as in other departments of public activ French initiative and enterprise are in forefront; while it is rather earious that first, and only, attempt of British enterpris in that direction has ended in rapid fail It is, however, a matter of sympathetic reg that the initial attempt by the friendly Fre nation at the commercial and indust development of this country, has been o rather unfortunate nature. The Beyrout-Dam cus-Mezeirib line which, though ipso fact a failure, can yet claim the honour of being pioneer, so to speak, of railroad enterprise Syria The first section from Damascus Mezerib was inaugurated on the Fre Republican Fête, 14th of July 1894; while second section from Damascus to Beyro was opened to traffic on the 3rd of Aug 1895. Both lines are of the narrow gauge ty having a width of 105 metre. The 1 from Beyrout to Damascus has a length 149 kilometres, while the Damascus Meze line is 100 kilometres long. Of the Beyro Damascus line 31 kilometres are of the e wheel type, and span the high ridges of 1 Lebanon. In an article last year, one of correspondents dwelt on the deficiencies this line, and its inherent incapacity to e with the requirements of the trade it built to serve, and the facts, since then, h illustrated the truth of his statement. This herent incapacity may be realized by t fact that some of the gradients are as ste as 7 centimetres per metre, the maximu railway inclination on record. The enormo consumption of coal which is said to quadrupled-the ton ex-waggon Beyrout co ing Frs. 30/35, the great tear and wear both rolling stock and fixed material, a the considerable loss of time, occasioned the inevitable slowness of the trains crossi the gradients, must necessarily condemn su a line to certain failure. A cursory surv of the history of this line is sufficient illustrate the facts of the case The origin promoters of this scheme are known as t Societe des Chemins de Fer Ottomane E nomique de Beyrouth-Damas-Hanran Biredjik sur L'Euphrate, a rather imposi name with a certain irony in the attribu Three years from the date of its inaug ration this company began to totter, al was on the verge of failure, when it oug salvation at the hands of the Société Batignolles. The latter took over the mi agement of the concern, undertaking to defr all the expenses against a lump-sum said be 15 million franes, hoping evidently make a profit on savings in the expenditu It was a sort of farming the exploitatio The period of the agreement was six year but at the end of the third year-a fat figure for the concern-the Batignolle in turn collapsed. Then came the real savio Mr. Vitalis of the "Regie Generale des Cl mins de Fer" He proposed to provide t necessary funds for building, for accou of the original concessionaires, the S ciété Economique, the Rayak-Homs-Ham Aleppo line, and against the creation such a rich resource, calculated to cont bute vastly to the increase of the receipts the narrow line, and the better management the united lines, he claimed an equal sha of the interests of the concern, halving bo revenue and expenditure. The bargain w a good one to both parties. The Régie p fitably employed its funds, made money the construction enterprise, and assured i profits on the exploitation of the narrow lin in which its interests were bound up f twenty five years, the term of the agreement while on the other hand the Societé Econ mique was lifted up from the verge of immine bankruptcy to the respectable position credit and solvency. But all this will n disprove the fact of the inherent inefficien of the narrow line. Certain defenders of th initiators of this scheme plead that, when was.conceived the country's needs were litnite and the agricultural and industrial condition were such as could not justify abroad line, fi less one that, with a long tunnel and other engineering works, would have involved a much larger cut lay of capital. But there was the evil of every shortsighted scheme, imma- tarely conceived and carried out. When, in its incipient stage, the traffic of the country was limited, the receipts were not sufficient to cover the abnormal cost of up keep and coal consumption etc.; and now that the subsid- iary line of Rayak-Aleppo has, even before its completion, given such an unexpected impetus to the development of the traffic, this narrow cogwheel line failed again, and demonstrated more clearly than ever its inher- ent incapacity. It had been thought that by doubling the rolling stock, and introducing powerful locomotives, the fast growing traffic would be satisfied, but the remedy can only prove to be a mere palliative for a radical evil. Indeed, the general concourse of opinion even among the railway officials themselves, was that all that such efforts were useless, and that the construction of a broad level line from here to Rayak was inevitable. The Manager of a well-known British Steamship Company, on being acquainted with the facts relating to our railways, made the very witty remark that the narrow cogwheel line, in its relation to the broad Rayak-Aleppo section, recalls the parallel of the story of Robinson Crusoe, who, having built too large a boat, had to dig a special channel for floating it. All the goods transported by the Aleppo line have had till now to be transhipped at the Rayak junction to the narrow line trucks, for ultimate transport to Beyrout, the only seaport terminus of the French lines in Syria.It has at last been decided to lay a broad line between Beyrout and Rayak. Sometime ago a staff of engineers was sent to survey the Hammana route, and it was found that, to avoid gradients, the base of the Keneisse mountain had to be penetrated, involving a tunnel length of about 4 kilometers. The cost has been estimated at about 20 million francs. Although it would be somewhat presumtuous to pass an opinion on a matter, that requires so much close and careful study, yet it would, we think, be legitimate to express the opinion that if no subterranean watercourses "poches d'eau" of any appreciable volume, be met with on the tunnel tract, the cost would be very considerably reduced.For our part we believe that when this line is completed the sanguine predictions respecting the importance of the traffic of the Aleppo listrict will be realized. One has only to con- sider the important development of trade in the interior, subsequent to the laying of the existing lines, to form an adequate idea of what further.extensions in the most fertile regions of northern Syria may produce. The railway Company his well seen how the de- velopment of agriculture and commerce, in the vast plains of Hauran and Homs Hama, and the adjoining parts, has been stimulated beyond every sanguine calculation, through the facili- ties of transport afforded by the railways. Formerly it used to cost the farmer on Hauran over 200 piastres, and perhaps mor, according to the distance, to transport on camel back a ton of grain; and very often, if he could afford to pay the cost, the limited number of camels sometimes caused ever this primitive means of transport to be unava lable. Now the cost has been reduced to less than the half for the outlying regions, and still less for the nearer places around Damascus ; and, irregular though the narrow line be, the transport by it, even of large quantities, can be counted upon;. though of course with a great deal of interrup- tion and delay. But this is not all. You have the security that is afforded by the railway against the tremendous risks of camel ransport, aggravated by the lavlesness prevailing in most of the agricultural plains of Syria. Comparisons between the arrivals of grain from Damascus and Hauran and Beyrout before and after the railway, present startling results. In the month of July last, when grain shipments are not quite in full swing yet, 13,000 tons were transported over the narrow line, and one cannot but think with wonder how only a few years ago before the ailway came into existence, Beyrout was an Insignificant port, in so far as exportation is concerned, and how, after the railway, it has in one leap risen to take its rank amongst the eading ports of the Ottoman Empire.

div.head: LORD CROMER'S RESIGNATION,
THE LONDON PRESS
div.p: One of the Conservative London newspapers blames the Government for Lord Cromer's ressignation. The "Tribune", of the 9th inst., remarks. "One of the cheaper prints which promptly fix the blame for everything urtoward that happens-from an earthquake in Jamaica to a shortage of work at Woolwich-on the shoulders of a Liberal Government, declared, on the morrow of Lord Cromer's resignation, that it was 'another unfortunate instance of the subtle anti-Imperial influence diffused by Liberal Governments.' And, of course, the name of the Premier was coupled, in a derogatory sense, with the resignation It was amusing, therefore, to find a more responsible organ of the Opposition yesterday referring to 'the mendacious prints' which have 'roundly asserted that Lord Cromer had been driven out of office-practically dismissed by the Prime Minister' For the ties between the two differing sheets are close and intimate."

div.head: THE BRITISH OCCUPATION.
div.p: Our position in Egypt will always call for an Army of Occupation; and it is not peculiar but rather natural that among his last duties Lord Cromer found it necessary to increase that Army. Considering the local problem only, there is no indication that the British garrison can be reduced in the near future. Its recent augmentation was due to the urbane and liberal institutions with which Lord Cromer has endowed Egypt, and to his constant desire to hide, as much as might be, for the susceptibilities of native opinion, the fact that we hold the country by the sword. British regiments are stationed in Cairo and Alexandria, not only to support our supremacy in the civil administration, but to protect a hundred and fifty thousand Europeans resident in the country. It is argued that we have no moral right to occupy Egypt, and that Europeans would be as safe there as in Turkey or Persia. To this we may reply that we have no moral right to occupy India, nor the French Tunis, nor the Germans Kiaochau, nor the Americans the Philippines, but we may rest assured that all these countries are the better for the presence of their respective overlords. It will also be admitted that if there were no British Army in this country its substitute would not be an Egyptian Army. There would undoubtedly be, as in the past, a Turkish Army, with, Egyptian, Nubian, and Sudanese soldiers. In preoccupation days, while the Turkish hand was strong the Viceroy's Army was, manageable; when the Turkish hand slackened, the fellah element broke bounds, and the Arabi rebellion of 1882 was the result, with its attendant massacre of Christians. From which fact we easily come to another, too often overlooked, namely, that the British in Egypt are no more alien that the Turks, and there can be no manner of doubt that the millions of peasants of Egypt prefer our overlordship with our justice to Turkish overordship and Turkish justice. This is the governing factor in the Egyptian problem, and only men obstinately blind to facts will refuse to accept it as axiomatic.

Sir Eldon Gorst, if he have the confidence of the people of Great Britain, will not deviate from the policy of resolution, sympathy, and prescience initiated in Napoleonic method by the genius of Lord Cromer. Those who think to find in him a weakling and an imifator, however, will be undeceived. There is that finesse in his character which aptly inaugurates an era of cordial co-operation if those most nearly concerned will accept him and his mission; but they waste their time if they hope that either cajolery of intimidation will affect his judgment. ("Morning Post").

div.head: FANATICISM IN MARIOUT
SHEIKH EL GERBI AND THE "TIMES."
div.p: Last week an article on the nationalist campaign, sent to the "Times" from Cairo, contained the following statement.

"For the moment the fortissimo of their (the Nationalists) exultations and threats has caused considerable alarm among the peaceable and law abiding elements of the population; and there is, unhappily, some reason for their fears. Sheikh El Gerbi-a half-witted fanatic carried away by his own eloquence- has been preaching inflammatory sermons in the Mariout district."

We received a visit from Sheikh el Gerbi yesterday. He is a benevolent looking person and does not by any means look half-writted. The Sheikh informs us that the statements of the "Times" are without foundation and that he is without any political or fanatical bias, but that from time to time he has gone to the Mariout district in order to instruct the backward folk of that region in the elements of religion. The Sheikh requests us to publish the following statement, which we have translated from the Arabic:

A month ago somebody brought a false accusation against me and when I became aware of the fact, I went to the Adviser of the Ministry of the Interior and asked him to open an enquiry into the case. I also sent a letter to the British Agency demanding an enquiry. There have been not only one but many informers against me. I have been awaiting for an enquiry to be held but up to now nothing has been done. On the 7th inst. whilst perusing "Al Moayad" I noticed an article reproduced from the "Times" wherein it was stated that I had made inflamamtory harangues at Mariont. It is for this reason that I demanded that an enquiry be made in that district. I have now been obliged to write to the Press to deny these accusations, for I am surprised that up to now no enquiry has been made. I wish it to be known that I will not be silent until the charges against me have been enquired into and justice be rendered. In such a case silence would be prejudicial to me and my interests.
Signed: ALY ABOU EL NOUR EL GERBIL

div.head: THE NOMENCLATURE OF THE STREETS OF ALEXANDRIA.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE "EGYPTIAN GAZETTE"
div.p: Sir,-I have read your interesting leading article in to-day's issue of the "Egyptian Gazette" with much appreciation and in most cases fully concur with the criticisms. As an old resident, therefore, I should like to make the following observations. In the first place you say that Rosetta-street is considered to be the old Canopic highway. I believe that there is no doubt that the main eastern road in ancient times was in this direction, but archæological authorities are not quite agreed upon the exact alignment of the road. Professor Botti placed it parallel to the existing road and somewhat to the south. In the case of the choice of a name for Sisters-street, Saba Banat as it is known in Arabic, there was a great conflict of opinion a few years ago. The reason was that the Arabs knew the road as the Rue Ibrahim, because Ibrahim Pasha first carried this street over the month of the Mahmoudieh Canal. The official name was Ibrahim but the popular name was the Seven Sisters Road, after the seven nuns, or less, who were the precursors of the existing charitable institution which does so much good both from a philanthropic and an educational point of view. Your remarks as to the needlessness of changing Frank-street to Rue de France are justified. Frank street had a historical significance in as much as that part of the city was the first quarter of Alexnadria to be inhabited by Europeans from the times of the Venetian merchants. It was altered to the Rue de France because an influential French member of the Alexandria Municipality wanted it to be called so.
In your leader you object to the heroic Gordon's name which bestowed on a little street, in which some of the houses do not bear the highest reputataion.

The Prince by right of birth is Prince of Asturias, but had the successor to the Spanish throne been a Princess she would not have been Princess of Asturias until the King had conferred the title on her.

The Heirs-Apparent have not always borne these titles, but were known formerly as First Infante or First Infanta. The title of Prince of Asturias was first granted by Juan I. of Castile in 1388 to his son (who afterwards became Henry III.) on his marriage with, Catalina, daughter of the Dake of Lancaster, and grand-daughter of Don Pedro I. of Castile and his morganatic wife Dona Maria of Padilla. For some years the Prince of Asturias had actual control over the province of that name, but this authority was withdrawn by Ferdinand and Isabella the Catholic on their uniting the Kingdoms of Castile and Aragon. Before the union of these kingdoms the heir to the throne bore the title of Prince of Gerona, which was founded by Ferdinand I. in 1414 for his son Alfonso VI, and the heir to the throne of Navarre was known after 1423 as the Prince of Viana. The Infante Don Juan, son of Ferdinand and Isabella, however, had two of these titles and also a new one. He was the Prince of Asturias, the Prince of Gerona, and the Prince of the New World

div.head: THE SHEM-BL NESSIM SCARE
div.p: A correpondent writes:- The feast of Shem- el-Nessim is over, and those people who have recently been s deeply disturbed by the anti- cipation of an outbreak of the part of the natives will take a deep breath of relief: There can be no doubt that the tension was for some weeks, in some quarters, xtreme, but on taking a dispassionate view of the situation, now that the occasion of danger is past, would it not seem the isolated misdemeanours of in- dividuals were to readily magnified into the heralds of a National storm; and the acts of violence perpetrated by a mixel mass of strikers together with the riff raff which are insepar ble from such bands in every country of the world, too easily assumed to represent the desires of a whole people ripe for rebellion

The letters, which have been published from various correspondents during the past few weeks, will amply testify as to, the reality of the agitation; It is always wise to show the world that we are prepared for any call which may be made upon our strength, but the loud assuarances of a certain pessimistic portion of the British community resident in Egypt that trouble was bound to come, are hardly calculated to lessen the task which is always before the Government, or to raise the standard of our prestige in the eyes of the native.

While it would be idle to deny that the spirit of Nationalism has been active in the towns for some time past, it must not be forgotten that the rural districts, are for the most part free from disaffection, or that in almost every case where rioting has take place, it has sprang from conflicts between low caste natives annd the lowest class Europeans. The Egyptian police have, as a body, given us no cause to doubt their loyalty, and while this remains the case we can rest assured that trouble, should it arise, would merely be local and more than likely to burn itself out in the locality in which it arose.

The statesman of Asia are well aware of the number of their subjects, know from history that the assumed difference in military quality is in part imaginary, and are profoundly convinced it may be from conceit, it may also be from a just perception of their own powers of thought-that on the whole their intellects are at least equal, both for reflection and for the practical work of life, to those of their arrogant rivals. The war has therefore, so to speak, immensely increased the self conceit of the East, as well as its self respect, and its annoyance at the sometimes assumed, but sometimes also real, contempt with which it is regarded by the West.

There are, however, in addition to those great causes, at least three others, each of them sufficient to create the keenest animosity. In the first place, Europeans, and more especially our countrymen, hardly understand the exasperation which is produced by the claim of the white intruders to be considered, not as friends or advisers, or even equal enemies, but as natural rulers gifted by heaven with the right to guide and control, and, we may add, tax, all black, brown, or yellow peoples with whom they are brought in contact. The whites claim, and have for a century exacted, the position of an aristocracy among races of other colours. The white man in an Asiatic State never accepts any other position than that of first, and that by right, not of his creed, nor even of his knowledge, but of some inherent. and, as it were, divinely granted superiority. He never consents to any lower position, and is, in fact, unable even to think of himself in any other. Many observers believe that this is the real cause of the readiness with which Asiatic tribes, when in revolt against white men or their influence, so constantly begin operations with massacre. The whites, they think, must be killed out, for, if not, even defeat will never coerce them into submission. (The French common folk thought just the same thing of their nobles when they expelled them, or mobbed them, or sent them to the guillotine.) The second subsidiary cause is the desire for exciting careers, careers bringing power and responsibility and praise, which the white men always seem to arrest. Whenever the latter are great in an Eastern State compar rative torpor falls upon all other aspirants. Military distinction, political distinction, even social distinetion, seem to be transferred from the natives of the country to aliens, who, even when they do not impose their laws on them, do impose their methods, their ideals, and, as a permanent reserve of force, their own picked men. That chance of rising to the top which in independent States vitalises a thousand ambitions and able men for every one who can succeed is taken away, as it were at a stroke, without a reason apparent to the people, and without a hope of any future alteration of system. A new and disagreeable aristocracy with real powers and capacities is introduced from outside into the body politic, in some cases with the most paralysing results. In India, for instance, where the process has for many obvious reasons become most nearly complete, Anglo-Indians would hardly admit the possibility of entrusting great buildings to native architects, though their originality in many departments of their art is past all dispute by the admission of European experts. It may be perfectly just, or even inevitable, to refuse the command of armies to brown or yellow soldiers but Asia has not forgotten Jenghis Khan, or for that matter, Kuroki. Millions of born soldiers are told, in effect, that the hope of supreme command is not for them. As we say, this may be inevitable - personally, we believe that it is - but it would be foolish because of that belief not to admit that the feeling, half of despair and half of indignation dwhich the practice must rouse within those millions is also inevitable. European influence in fact, when predominant in any State in Asia, closes or dwarfs the healthiest, or at any rate the fiercest, ambitions. And thirdly, there is the question of money. We in the West all say that we wish the darker races whom we govern to grow rich, that we show them the way at least to that end, and that we take nothing in return beyond our just wages. The Asiatic retorts:-"Be your motives what they may, you take all the best positions, all the richest 'concessions', and most of those resources out of which we, if we were left to our livess, might most easily grow rich. You want, even if you do not always get, our highly paid appointinents, our mines,and our means of swift communication, all of them very profitable and desirable things which ought to belong to us." For, remember, the Asiatic does not admit that he is naturally his rival's inferior e en in scientific enterprise. It follows that as the East advances, becomes more educated, more intelligent, and, owing to the Japanese, victories

more hopeful, it becomes also more conscious of a wish that the intruder should go away,- bould not necessarily be exterminated, but hould cease to be an obstacle in its own path. These things, which we have very briefly, and probably very imperfectly, expressed, are, we mre convinced, among the principal causes of Eastern unrest.

There is one more cause which we must not omit, because our readers will expect it to be discussed, but to which Englishmen probably attach exaggerated importance, -namely, the difference of creed. This exists, and in some places in a powerful moving cause of insurrection, but it is not quite so powerful or so general in its nature as is commonly imagined. The Chinese undoubtedly dislike native Christian converts, as being persons sure in the end to upset their own highly valued civilisation. But it is extremely doubtful whether they object to white men being Christian, or care at all about the difference between the European faith and their own. They probably regard Christianity as a false system, but with no more acerbity than European Protestants regard Roman Catholicism. It is all wrong, they think, but in religion every one must judge for himself. In India Hindus cannot in theory condemn Christianity, admitting as they do that for each caste its special faith is the necessary truth, and nothing in Christianity specially provokes or excites them. The Mussulman no doubt thinks everywhere that God has given him the right to rule, and has placed with him the depositum fidei; but he knows that heaven can wait even better than man and if it is convenient he will await the declaration of heaven's will. He does not want to be shot because the doctors of his faith proclaim on every Friday that it is the first duty of their disciples to risk the shooting on behalf of the supremacy of their Prophet. On the subject of creeds Europe and Asia have repeatedly found a modus ricendi, and an inter continental war of religions is hardly more probable than an inter-State war on the same ground in modern Europe. The real grounds of dislike are more concrete, and, if not more reasonable, are more easily to be appreciated by the average European mind,

We need hardly act that use we realise that the East would like to do without the European and to rule itself, we by no means admit that the East could perform the task. On the contrary, we believe that it would fail utterly, and that if we were to leave India and Egypt to govern themselves, we should thereby immensely increase the sum of human misery, and give no compensating benefits. The Eastern peoples, in spite of their intellectual gifts, only understand the establishment of one form of government, and that is despotism tempered by anarchy and rebellion. But this is a form of government which is intolerable if we are to hold intercourse with the East, and trade demands such intercourse as a necessity. Japan cannot be regarded as proof to the contrary. The way in which Japan shook off her seclusion, and voluntarily adopted the most vital parts of Western civilisation, shows that at heart she is not an Asiatic Power.

La bonne tendance du marché, gnalée à la fin de la semaine dernière, s'est non seulement accentuée, mais a fini par se traduire et un véritable mouvement de hausse partir de Samedi matin. A l'ouverture, il ny avait rien de particulier en vue, mais áved les bor nes exportations données en noté pour les journées de Jeudi et de Vendredi et les bonnes nouvelles d'Amérique, la fermeté se faisait remarquer. Seulement, il y avait quelque chose depeu encou rageant en l'air et vers midi les dispositions étaient sur le point de se modifier, quand tout à coup des ordres importants d'achat, surtout pour la récolte actuelle, ont commencé à nous venir et ont fini par nous valoir une hausse de 15/32 sur le Mai et 1 4 de tallari sur le Novem bre. On a attribué ces ordres,an Cain, mais on ne saurait dire si, en l'espèce, il est agi, de rachats du découvert on d'achats péculatifs stimulés. par la bonne tenue des jours précé dents; en tous cas, cela n'a aucune in portance, le fait important étant qu'une opcasica propice venait de se présenter à nos haussiers qui ne se sont pas faits faute d'en profiter.

Jusque-là, cependant, il n'y avail rien de bien extraordinaire, car si surprise reelle il y a eu, cette surprise ne nous a été servie que mardi, à la reprise des affaires après le chôma ge de lundi à l'occasion du Cham el Nesiim. En effet, ce jour-là il y a eu de l'excitation et le Mai a été porté presque d'emble à 20 tallaris, tandis que,, de son côté, le Novembre s'inscrivait à 19 3/4., Vraiment, c'était trop, aussi la légère réaction notée en clôture a été considérée comme naturelle. Nous ajouterons même que si elle n'a pas été plus marquée, ce n'est que parce que la lutte qui venit de se livrer avait été trop vive et que quelques haussiers acharnés avaient tout fait pour sou- tenir les cours, circonstance qui a permis à leurs confrères, mienx inspirés qu'eux, de leur passer lears paquets.

Au fond, il y avait scission dans camp haussier et ce sont précisément les délections qui venaient d'être signalées qui ont été la cause principale du revirement qui s'est pré dait à partir de mercredi. Affaiblis romme nombre, les acheteurs restés sur la brèche sont trouvés être insuffisants et peut-être déjà trop surchargés pour absorber tout equi s'offrait à la vente aussi, la perte éprouvée dans la matinée de mercredi d'an demi tallari pour le Mai et de 3/8 pour le Novembie n'a-t. elle étonné personne.

Hier, pourtant, et malgré une certaine dimi nution dans les exportations et malgré un pen de calme en Amérique, la tenue a été meilleure et la séance s'est même terminée ave un petite hausse de 1/32 à 1/16; mais, aujour d'hui, la faiblesse a de nouveau, pris le dessus et nous a fait reculer de 1/4 de tallari sur toute la ligne, le tout basé sur la différence sensible entre les prévisions et les embarquements réels de la semaine, qui a engendré un désir intense de réalisations chez quelques détenteurs.

Maintenant, tout compté, le Novembre, en clôturant à 19 1/8, n'a fait que perdre ce qu'il avait gagné dans l'entre-temps, tandis que le Mai, qui a fini au même cours, reste quand theme en avance de 1/4 de tallari sur la se maine passée

Au fond done, il n'y aurait eu aucun mal, sauf pour ceux qui se sont laissés emballer au plus fort de la manoeuvre; mais il n'en est pas moins vrai que l'hésitation, qui semble regner pour le moment, constitue un sujet de préceu- pation pour les plus gros détenteurs de contats, à cause du pli qu'elle pourrait prendre avec la diminution, prévue dans les exportations de la) semaine prochaine et qui, indubitablement ne sanrait laisser indifférents les petits spécia teira engagés à la hausse.

Il est vrai que dans certains quartiers on prétend que la filature anglaise est anxie se d'acheter de l'Fgyptien aux cours actuels En théorie, peut être; mais en prátique nous ne voyons pas ces bonnes dispositions prendre -corps et consistance.

Maintenant, pour revenir au marché, nous dirons que, comme ensemble, il y a encore eu, assez d'activité sur l'ancienne récolte; par contre, le Novembre a été moins animé, Toute-- fois, pour ce qui regarde ce dernier, la tenue a été plus satisfaisante en ce sens que, ni à la hausse, ni à la baisse, les fluctuations n'ont été exagérées ou de nature à effrayer le marché.

Signalons en outre la divergence d'opinion qui commence à se dessiner au sujet de la nou- velle récolte. Nous avons déjà relevé dans nos pré cédentes revyes le fait que l'idée se répandait que le Novembre en lui-même était trop cher; aujourd'hui, poor lui faire contre poids, on-dit que dans tous les cas il offre moins de risques à l'acheteur que l'ancienne récolte et que si par la réussite de la nouvelle récolte améri- caine au point de vue qualité il est sujet peut- être au danger d'un fort recpl, il faudra bien du temps avant que ce fait ne se vérifie. Et que, de plus, on ne saurait parler d'une éven tualité pareille quand sur le tapis il est encore question de gros réensemensehents et de man- que de bonnes graines,

Cette dernière phrase résume les nouvelles d'Amérique, car en dehors de cela les dépêches de New-York n'ont rien signalé pour justifier la hausse de l'américain. Comme il y a arrêt, il est à supposer qu'il y a déjà amélioration dans la question du temps.

A quand le tour des dépêches annonçant que les fortes pluies ont été favorables à a plante en lui faisant prendre des racines plus profon des, ce qui la rendra plus apte à traverser la période de sécheresse qui se produit en Juillet et en Août

Et pour finir, signalons le fait regrettable qui s'est produit et consistant dans la suspen- sion d'une maison d'exportation, suspension qu'on ne s'explique pas dans les circonstances actuelles du marché, étant donné que depuis longtemps s véritable position était à la baisse. Espérons dans tous les cas qu'un arran- gement pourra être conglu avec ses créanciers. Le marché du disponible a été assez satistai- sant comme activité..

Quant aux prix, la cote officielle nous signale ane hausse de 5/8 de tallari pour les Mit Affifi, cé qui est d'accord avec les contrats. Les prove- nances Haute-Egypte ont été notées en hausse de 1/2 tallari aussi, mais les Joannovich n'ont subi aucun changement.
Au lieu des 2500 balles prévues, les exporta- tions e se sont élevées qu'à 2200 balles et cela a jeté du froid sur le marché.

Pour ce qui est de la semaine prochaine, il y a divergence dans les appréciations, mais généra lement on est convaincu que nous fotberons dans la note modérée, quoique toujours avec des embarquements supérieurs à ceux de l'année dernière qui n'ont été que de 6800 balles pour la même période.

A l'exception des actions de l'Union foncière de la Banque d'Orient et de la Banque d'Athè nes qui sont rechereliées, le reste de la cote libre accuse un léger recul.

L'amélioration, dont quelques unes de nos meilleures valeurs avaient profité à Londres et à Paris, a attiré sur ces places un flot de titres qui ont nécessairement provoqué un fléchisse- ment important des cours. Au Stock Exchange la National Bank perd ainsi près d'une livre à 23 1/2 contre 24 3,8 la semaine dernière, l'Agricultural et la Daira Sanieh 1,8 à 8 5/8 et 15 3/8 respectivement. Les fonds d'Etat égyptiens sont également atteints par la baisse En revanche la New Egyptian gagne 3/16 à 1 1/4 sur la nouvelle de la distribution d'un dividende intérimaire de 10%. A Paris la Banque d'Athènes fléchit à 127 en perte de 3 francs et le Crédit foncier Egyptien à 725 en. perte de 5 francs sur te semaine dernière. Par contre le Crédit franco Egyptien avance 144 en gain de 9 francs. Bien que le dernier bilan de la Banque d'Angleterre accuse une légère diminution dans la réserve des billets ainsi qu'une moins value de £200,000 dans l'encaisse, la proportion des réserves aux engagements progresse de 45 1/4 à 46 3,4%. Cette brillante situation et la réduction du taux de l'escompte libre attestent une fois de plus que la détente monétaire va en s'accentuant

De même à Berlin le taux de l'escompte libre cote 4 1,8% contre un taux officiel de 5 1/2 % Le bilan mensuel de la Banque de France confirme cette appreciation, il constate une réduction de 70 millions du niveau du porte- feuille et une diminution de 15 millions pour les avances sur titres

L'action Comptoir Financier et Commercial nous est renseignée aujourd'hui de Londres à 4 3/4 en perte de 3/8 de livre, la part de fon- dateur est négligée à £5; les bruits, les plus extraordinairement fâcheux continuent à cir- euler sur le compte de cet établissement, ce qui a amené certains détenteurs de ces actions à offrir leurs titres jusqu'au prix ridiculement bas de £4 1/2, malgré les prescriptions du Comité. Il nous semble être dans le vrai en disant que tous ces bruits alarmistes ne repo- sent sur aucun fondement sérieux, et sont probablement répandus à dessein par les enne-
mis de cette société.

Après d'excellents débuts la spéculation semble vouloir délaisser les Ritz Hotels qui étaient jusqu'ici un de ses titres favoris. L'assem- Blée générale de cette société à rejeté l'option de la Nile Land qui lui offrait 90,000 mètres de son terrain du Garden city, au prix de L.F. 5 le métré payable en action de la Ritz Hotel. Elle a par contre approuvé le projet de conversion des 5.000 parts de fonda- teurs en 100,000 actions ordinaires de £1, soit 20 actions ordinaires pour une part de fondateur. Cet échange parait avoir été mal interprété, par beaucoup d'actionnaires, et par le pablie en général, car l'on considère que la Société débute avec des frais de premier établissement de plus de £130.000 sur un capital émis de 150.000, ou en d'autres termes qu'elle donne à ses fondateurs, avant même qu'elle n'ait commencé à fonctionner des actions de capital pour les deux tiers de ce ospital, sans que ceux-ci aient eu à payer quoi que ce soit.

Avant hier soir à 5 heures a eu lieu l'As semblée générale extraordinaire des actionnaj res de la Banque Nationale. Elle a approuvé Is proposition présentée par le Conseil de por- ter le capital de Lat. 3.000.000 à Lat. 3,500,000 par la création de 50.000 actions nouvelles de 10 Lat. chacune. Ultérieu- tement, le Conseil d'administration fera con- ntre la date et les conditions de Vé- mission. On vient d'émettre à Londres pour un million de livres d'obligations de la Ban que Agricole au taux de 90, avee intérêt à 31/2 %. L'escompte libre à Londres a fléchi, avant- hier, de 1/8 & 3% et s'est maintenu hie à ce taux. A Paris, le Crédit Foncier Egyptien a re tionné, avant-hier. de 2 franes à 728, tanilis que la Banque d'Athènes est remontée de 3 franes à 130, Hier, la Bourse de Paris étuit fermée à l'occasion de la fête de l'Ascension

Ici, le marché est impressionné par la baisse de nos valeurs dirigeantes à Londres. Cette dépression a été évidemment déterminée par des ordres de vente transmis d'Egypte elle est la résultante d'opérations d'arbitrage t surtout de réalisations effectuées après la petis reprise de ces jours derniers.

La séancea été toutefois relativement calme. Toutes les offres en National Bank et Agricole oht trouvé aisément leur contr partie. Ce qui est rassurant, c'est qu'il y a de acheteurs sérieux, en très petit nombre il est vrai, mais il s'en présentera beaucoup
d'importants-si la baisse s'accentue dans de fortes proportions.
La National Bank, que nous avions laissés avant hier à 24 3/16, a clitur à 27 9/16 5/8 L'Agricole, plus résistante, sest tassée à 9/16-5/8.
